questions.prompt: A producer writes value, then sets flag, with no fence. A consumer in another block sees the flag set. What can it read from value?
options: Possibly the old value: the two writes may become visible out of order
questions.explanation: Relaxed memory models allow the reordering; a fence (or release/acquire atomics) prevents it.

options: Waits for all threads in the grid
Orders this thread's memory writes so earlier ones are visible device-wide before later ones
questions.explanation: It's an ordering point, not a barrier: nobody waits.

questions.prompt: Why can't you build a grid-wide barrier by having every block spin on a global counter?
options: If not all blocks fit on the GPU at once, running blocks wait for blocks that can never be scheduled: deadlock

questions.prompt: Which are legitimate ways to get a grid-wide synchronisation point?
options: End the kernel and launch another
Spinning in every block on a counter, in an ordinary launch

questions.prompt: In the last-block pattern, how does a block know it's the last one?
options: The atomicAdd on the counter returns gridDim.x − 1 to it
questions.explanation: Block indices say nothing about finishing order; the atomic ticket does.

questions.prompt: Why can't the GW-1 simulator reproduce memory-visibility races?
options: It runs blocks one at a time, so writes are always visible in program order
questions.explanation: It does randomise block order, which catches ordering assumptions, but not visibility bugs.
